questions.question: What does a foreground process do to the terminal?

options.text: Blocks it until the process completes
Runs it silently with no output

explanation.correct: A foreground process occupies the terminal and blocks all other input until it finishes.
explanation.why: A describes background, C is incorrect, D is background with redirected output.

questions.question: Which symbol runs a command in the background?

explanation.correct: The ampersand (&) at the end of a command sends it to the background and frees the terminal immediately.
explanation.why: # is comments, | is pipe, $ is variable prefix.

questions.question: What is a Linux repository?

options.text: A local folder for storing scripts
A trusted online source for downloading verified software packages
A database of EC2 instance configurations
A backup of your EC2 instance

explanation.correct: A repository is a trusted, verified online source that the package manager uses to fetch and install software safely.
explanation.why: It is analogous to a Play Store for Linux — verified, safe, centralized.

questions.question: Which package manager is used on Amazon Linux 2023?

explanation.correct: Amazon Linux 2023 uses dnf (Dandified YUM) as its default package manager.
explanation.why: apt is for Ubuntu/Debian, brew is macOS, pip is Python packages.

questions.question: What does the STAT code 'Z' mean in ps aux output?

options.text: Process is running at high speed
Process has finished but hasn't been cleaned up by its parent

explanation.correct: Z stands for Zombie — the process has completed but its parent hasn't called wait() to remove it from the process table.
explanation.why: Zombie processes consume no CPU or memory — just a PID slot.

questions.question: What two pieces of information does Linux display when you start a background process?

explanation.correct: Linux shows [Job ID] and Process ID (PID) when a process starts in the background.
explanation.why: Example: [1] 4823 — [1] is Job ID, 4823 is PID.

questions.question: Which command lists all background jobs in the current terminal session?

explanation.correct: The 'jobs' command (lowercase j) lists all background jobs with their job IDs and status.
explanation.why: ps shows system-wide processes, top is interactive monitor, bg moves a job to background.

questions.question: What does the command 'fg %2' do?

options.text: Brings background job number 2 to the foreground

explanation.correct: fg followed by %N brings the background job with job ID N to the foreground terminal.
explanation.why: The % sign indicates job number, not PID.

questions.question: What keyboard shortcut terminates a foreground process?

explanation.correct: Ctrl+C sends a SIGINT (interrupt) signal to the foreground process, terminating it.
explanation.why: Ctrl+Z suspends (pauses) the process, Ctrl+D sends EOF, Ctrl+X is not a process signal.

questions.question: On which port does SFTP operate?

explanation.correct: SFTP runs over SSH on port 22. It is SSH File Transfer Protocol — not FTP which uses port 21.
explanation.why: Port 80 is HTTP, 443 is HTTPS, 21 is legacy FTP (unencrypted).

questions.question: What does the '-y' flag do in 'sudo yum install docker -y'?

options.text: Runs the command as a background process
Automatically answers YES to all prompts

explanation.correct: The -y flag auto-confirms all prompts, allowing unattended installation without manual interaction.
explanation.why: Essential for automation scripts where no one is present to type 'y'.

questions.question: What is the correct way to install Docker on Ubuntu EC2?

explanation.correct: Ubuntu uses apt as its package manager. docker.io is the Ubuntu package name for Docker.
explanation.why: yum and dnf are for Amazon Linux/RHEL, brew is for macOS.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'systemctl start' and 'systemctl enable'?

options.text: start launches the service now; enable makes it auto-start at every boot
start is for user services; enable is for system services
enable is required before start can work

explanation.correct: 'start' runs the service immediately for the current session. 'enable' tells systemd to start the service automatically on every future reboot.
explanation.why: On EC2, you almost always need both — start to run now, enable so it survives reboots.

questions.question: A background process is still printing messages to your terminal even though you used &. What is the reason?

options.text: Background processes automatically use a different terminal
Linux does not detach standard output/error from the terminal by default
The process switched itself to foreground

explanation.correct: Even in the background, a process's stdout and stderr remain connected to the terminal by default. Linux does not auto-detach them.
explanation.why: Solution: redirect output with > file.log to silence terminal printing.

questions.question: What does 'ps aux' show that 'ps' alone does not?

options.text: All processes for all users including daemon processes

explanation.correct: The 'a' flag shows all users, 'u' adds user info, 'x' includes daemons (processes not attached to any terminal).
explanation.why: Plain 'ps' only shows processes in your current terminal session.

questions.question: What keyboard shortcut suspends (pauses) a foreground process without killing it?

explanation.correct: Ctrl+Z sends SIGTSTP which suspends the process, placing it in Stopped (T) state. It can then be resumed with fg or bg.
explanation.why: Ctrl+C kills it, Ctrl+D sends EOF, Ctrl+S freezes terminal scrolling.

questions.question: What does the STAT modifier '+' indicate in a process status?

options.text: Process is running in the foreground, attached to the terminal

explanation.correct: The '+' modifier means the process is in the foreground process group — attached to a controlling terminal.
explanation.why: For example, R+ means actively running in the foreground. Without '+', the process is in the background.

questions.question: Which command sends a suspended job back to the background?

explanation.correct: bg %N resumes a suspended (stopped) job and runs it in the background without bringing it to the foreground.
explanation.why: fg brings to foreground, jobs lists, resume is not a valid Linux command.

questions.question: When connecting FileZilla to EC2 and it shows 'Server refused our key', what is the most likely cause?

options.text: Duplicate or incorrect PEM key file in FileZilla SFTP settings

explanation.correct: FileZilla stores keys and key conflicts — having duplicate entries or the wrong key file — cause key rejection errors.
explanation.why: Fix: go to Edit > Settings > SFTP, remove duplicates, re-add the correct .pem file.

questions.question: What is the correct 'ps aux' column that shows process state?

explanation.correct: The column is named 'STAT' in ps aux output. It shows a code (R, S, D, T, Z) indicating the current process state.
explanation.why: This is a specific Linux field name — memorize it for exam questions.

questions.question: What happens to a zombie process if its parent process is killed?

options.text: The zombie is adopted by init (PID 1) which will clean it up
The zombie continues running as an orphan

explanation.correct: When a parent process dies, its orphaned children (including zombies) are re-parented to init (PID 1), which calls wait() to clean them up.
explanation.why: This is why killing the parent of many zombies often resolves zombie accumulation.

questions.question: What does 'sudo yum install docker -y > install.log &' accomplish?

options.text: Installs Docker in foreground and logs errors only
Installs Docker in background, redirects all output to install.log, frees the terminal
Creates a log file and then installs Docker
Installs Docker silently with no log

explanation.correct: The > redirects stdout to install.log (creating the file if needed), and & runs the entire command in the background — terminal is free while installation proceeds.
explanation.why: This is a real-world DevOps pattern for running long installs without blocking automation pipelines.

questions.question: What is the difference between Job ID and Process ID?

options.text: Job ID is assigned by the kernel; PID is assigned by the shell
Job ID is local to the current shell session; PID is system-wide and unique across the OS
They are the same number shown in different formats
Job ID is for background processes; PID is only for foreground

explanation.correct: Job ID is a sequential number (1, 2, 3) assigned by your shell to track jobs in that session. PID is assigned by the OS kernel and is unique system-wide at any given time.
explanation.why: Two different terminal sessions can both have a job #1, but no two running processes share the same PID.

questions.question: Which STAT code indicates a process waiting for hardware like disk I/O and cannot be interrupted?

explanation.correct: 'D' means Uninterruptible Sleep — the process is waiting for hardware (disk, network) and cannot be interrupted or killed until the hardware responds.
explanation.why: Unlike 'S' (interruptible sleep), a 'D' process cannot be killed with kill -9 and must wait for the hardware.

questions.question: A developer runs 'systemctl enable nginx' but forgets 'systemctl start nginx'. What is the result?

options.text: nginx starts immediately and also at every boot
nginx is registered to auto-start at next boot but is NOT running right now
nginx starts but will not restart after reboot
An error is thrown — enable requires the service to be running first

explanation.correct: 'enable' only sets up auto-start for future reboots. It does not start the service immediately. You must separately run 'systemctl start' to run it now.
explanation.why: This is a common production mistake — service looks configured but isn't actually running.

questions.question: What does the 'Sl' STAT code mean for a process like Docker?

explanation.correct: 'S' = sleeping, 'l' (lowercase) = multi-threaded. Services like Docker and MySQL use multiple threads and show 'Sl'.
explanation.why: Note: lowercase 'l' is multi-threaded, uppercase 'L' is locked pages in memory.

questions.question: Which SCP command uploads an entire local folder to EC2?

explanation.correct: The -r flag enables recursive copy for directories. The -i flag specifies the key pair file.
explanation.why: Without -r, scp only copies single files and will fail silently or error on directories.

questions.question: What package manager would you use on a Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 EC2 instance?

explanation.correct: RHEL 8 and later use dnf as the default package manager. RHEL 7 and earlier used yum.
explanation.why: rpm is the low-level package format, not a full package manager with dependency resolution.

questions.question: You want to view all processes consuming CPU across all users. Which is the best real-time monitoring tool?

explanation.correct: 'top' provides a real-time, continuously updated view of processes sorted by CPU usage. ps aux is a one-time snapshot.
explanation.why: For real-time monitoring, top (or htop) is better than ps aux which requires re-running manually.

questions.question: An EC2 instance has 200 zombie processes. What is the primary risk?

options.text: High CPU consumption causing performance degradation
High memory usage causing OOM errors
Exhausting available PID slots in the process table
Filling the disk with zombie process files

explanation.correct: Zombie processes hold a PID slot in the process table. If the table fills up, the system cannot create new processes, causing failures.
explanation.why: Zombies themselves use no CPU or memory — the danger is PID slot exhaustion.
